utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone, the Interpreters note. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, will you please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, were there any weapons in that house on that date, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in my house, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In your father's house, to your knowledge, were there any weapons in that house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I was aware, there were no weapons, the four houses that we owned, that is, my neighbours and us, there were no weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you left the house and you moved toward a certain part of the town. Now, as you went outside the house, what did you see outside in the streets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw civilians moving in that direction. There were some soldiers, there was a tank in the street, there was what I called a Sumatka [phoen], which was a blue police car, and there were soldiers in uniforms. I remember the camouflage uniforms, both army uniforms and police uniforms. And we walked along in that direction. I didn't notice any problems; I saw nothing terrible going on. The children were crying, they were afraid of the tanks, but there was no problem as far as I was concerned. I thought that they would just conduct the search and return us home, as they said they would.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, did you serve in the military? .

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did serve my military service in 1984/1985, in Podgorica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What sort of speciality did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the anti-aircraft artillery, 20-millimetre, and I was a Private First Class in the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you have supervisory authority over any personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I had a unit made up of six people. As a private first class, that was what I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So these six people were under your authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that when you went out into the street you saw a tank. That tank, was it familiar to you, based on your military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't tell what the make of the tank was, but it did belong to the Yugoslav People's Army anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned that you saw some police vehicles, and I would like now to have an exhibit provided to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: This exhibit would be marked as the next in order, which I believe for the Prosecution is 3/80. This would be 3/80A and 3/80B. I have copies for the Defence, and copies have previously been provided for the Judges. This is what will go to the Defence and this is what will go to the witness. Now, if you would first, please, allow the witness to look at both of those photos. Now, those photos that you're given, could the first one, A, be put on the screen. It says "A" on the front and on the side.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you will look in the background at the vehicle that appears to have some type of barrel sticking out from it, do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it. That was the vehicle. And there was another vehicle, I thought it was an anti-aircraft one, the barrels were longer, but it was a similar type of vehicle and I seem to recall this now, although I might not have said it to begin with, the barrel was longer but there was this vehicle as well and they passed by.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you would put B on the screen as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Is this a similar type vehicle as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are similar vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you also mentioned that there were people in the street who had camouflage uniforms. Did you recognise those uniforms from your time in the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were camouflage uniforms of the type that we called camouflage uniforms in the Yugoslav People's Army, and there was the olive-green/grey type, and there were also police camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And the police camouflage uniforms were of what colour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were dark blue, light blue, a mixture, but those colours generally. Some patches were a little darker. Whereas the other ones were green, of a light yellow colour, greeny colour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were there different kinds of the green camouflage uniforms or were they all the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some were a little darker than others; others were lighter. And then there were the olive-green/grey uniforms, depending on who was wearing what. But I know that particular uniform from the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, these ones that were dark blue and light blue camouflage, when you were in the military, had you seen those uniforms in the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I had because I was at the Golubovac airport once for exercises and they had that type of military uniform, and those were similar uniforms to that. They had blue uniforms, the soldiers at the airport, and they were of the same colour, as far as I'm able to remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I'd also ask that the witness be provided with an exhibit which I have marked 3/81. Copies have previously been provided for the Court, and I would ask that copies be given to the Defence. If that could be put on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, the people that you saw in the street on the 30th of May wearing uniforms, do you recognise that as one of the kinds of camouflage uniforms that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did recognise this. I call this the camouflage uniform of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise anyone in that picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recollect, this is Mr. Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would you point to who is Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This man here [indicates] with his arm raised.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what was this area of town that you were moving toward with these other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We call it Skela, and that's where we came and we were all there together. And there was a slaughterhouse there, Klanica. There were lots of us there. And I noticed buses coming and going, taking people off, as I approached.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated there were a lot of people there. Did you recognise any of those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of them were my neighbours from the same street, so I knew many of them personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened, then, when you had been gathered at this slaughterhouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After a short period of time, a soldier came up and said that the women and children should stand apart with the elderly people, over the age of 65, and that the rest of us were to move towards the buses. At that time there was a lot of crying, and I started to cry too because we didn't know where we were going. I thought the worst was going to happen. And I hugged my children and my wife, and my father came up to me, told me to be careful, not to make problems and that everything would be all right, that I should behave well. He gave me a little money, I put it in my pocket. I don't know how much he gave me. My wife also gave me her golden jewellery, and she put it in the pocket of my jacket. The children were crying. I just said, "Look after our children. Don't worry. Everything will be fine." Of course, this was a great time of stress for me because I didn't know where I was going, but we sort of felt a premonition. We went into the bus, we had to bow our heads and not to look around. What happened to my family afterwards, I did not know, until I returned from Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you were taken from this area to Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Before that my father was 55, he came up to the guard, he was supposed to go with us but he showed a paper saying that he had work assignments and they said he could go back. But he is pale, he has a pale complex, and they thought he might be ill. My sister's husband, my brother-in-law who was for Kozarac, showed them a piece of paper as well and they sent him back. So they weren't taken off together with us. My brother-in-law was 36 or 37, but he was returned on that occasion as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What time of the day or what part of the day was it that you arrived at Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It had begun to grow dark. I don't remember the exact time. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you arrived at Omarska camp, where did the bus stop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bus stopped in front of what we referred to Mujo's dormitory. They told us to get out, to put our hands up behind our backs, and to stand up against the wall. We had to stand up against the wall until -- and they searched us. After the search, a man wrote down my name and surname and my father's name, and when I had finished that, at that time I was sent to the pista.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If I could ask you to speak just a little bit slower, that would assist the interpreters and the court reporter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well. I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that when you got off the bus that you were searched. Did you have to assume any particular position when you were searched?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I had to stand with my legs astride, I had to put up my three fingers and touch the wall that way, and that's how they searched me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the search, what, if anything, was taken from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at that moment they took everything away I had in my pockets. My father had given me 300 or 500 marks, I forget how much. My wife's gold jewellery was taken away and so were my cigarettes, because I had some cigarettes on me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was this money or jewellery ever returned to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never. It was never returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you arrived at this place that was the entry to Mujo's room. What building are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The building is where the offices were, the restaurant, and so on. And afterwards we referred to as Mujo's room.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You also indicated that from there you went out onto the pista. What happened while you were on the pista?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Afterwards other buses came, and I heard this other bus come. And there was some beating...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: ... I think the witness said. After a certain time had elapsed, we went inside and Kvocka addressed us, and he introduced himself, said he was responsible for us, something along those lines, that everything would be fine, that there were no problems, that we would be questioned, and then that we would be returned home. And later on we went to that dormitory which we referred to as Mujo's room. After about an hour or two had gone by, a bus came, another bus came, and that bus was from my street as well, and two young men were beaten up. They were all bloody. And they just said that they had been to the SUP and that they had been beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If I could ask you to stop there for a moment. Where were you when Kvocka addressed you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment I was at the pista.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: This person Kvocka who addressed you, did you know him from before the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How was he dressed when he addressed you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had a police uniform on, and he had a pistol, and I can't remember whether he had a rifle on that occasion or not. I cannot recall. He said that everything would be all right, that we would be interrogated and then we would be returned home.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated that he introduced himself and then after that he told you something to the effect that he was responsible for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is how I understood his remark. I think he also gave his name at that moment, but I'm not quite sure of that. But later, in any case, I learnt that his name was Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, when you think he gave his name at that moment, do you mean his first name and last name, or just part of a name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he said first and last name, but I was in such a state that I didn't pay attention to all these details, and I couldn't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Then you indicated you went into Mujo's room and two young men came in and they were beaten up. What were the names of these young men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)and Hamdija Brkic. (redacted) (redacted), and Hamdija was close to the club up there. I knew them. Hamdija wore rubber boots. He was not at all active.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were also Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated that he was not at all active. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean he was not interested in politics at all. He was out of a job. He would just come and paint people's houses; he would just work for a living. So he wasn't active in any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you can recall at all, about what time was it that you were actually taken into Mujo's room that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was getting cool, so it was about 12.00 or before 12.00 that we were taken inside. I'm not sure of the time. But it was already night-time and getting cooler.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long had you been on the pista before Kvocka came and addressed you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly an hour and a half or two.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was it still daylight? Was it dusk? Was it night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was dusk, and night had started to fall. I think that the lights were already coming on. I seem to remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, how long did you stay in Mujo's room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next morning I was taken out to the pista again.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you went to the pista the next morning, what did you see on the pista? What armed personnel did you see on the pista?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were military men, I cannot remember whether that was that same day, they were on two sides. But later I know they were there, seven days later. But a long time has gone by so I can't remember. There were guards, as were normally there on the pista. We sat there, waiting to be interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So there were guards and then there were these military men; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The military men that you speak of, were these men that you came to recognise as regular camp personnel at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I later recognised among them some of them as camp personnel. Before that I didn't know any of them. Later on I recognised them, and I know them by name.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, when you were on the pista this day or the next day, did you notice any special units there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think those were special units in this police car. They wore dark blue camouflage uniforms, and I think they belonged to the special police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What kind of police car was it that they had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had a blue car and a large machine-gun on top. There was one on the left and one on the right; they were parked there. In front was the restaurant and behind was the wall of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Just a while ago you were shown two photographs, 3/80A and B of blue vehicles that you identified. Do you recall that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The vehicles that you saw with this special unit, were they the same type of vehicles as on those photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they were the same type of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long did this special unit stay at Omarska, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not long, but I can't tell you exactly. Seven days, maybe a little more. But I cannot say exactly for how long.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: During this seven days that they were in the camp, where were you being held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time I was at the pista during the daytime, and in the evening to sleep I went to the restaurant or upstairs, depending on where there was room, upstairs in the hangar building or in the restaurant. But in the morning we had to go back to the pista.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you observe of the conduct of these special units towards the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember once a shot was fired when we were lining up for lunch. A shot was fired and a man was wounded in the hand. His name is Ilija Musanovic, and he was from my street. I remember that incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The person who wounded him, was this person a regular camp personnel or was it a member of this special unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see that person who did that, but I think that they were these special units.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the time this special unit was in Omarska, what differences, if any, did you notice between the way they treated the detainees and the way the regular camp personnel treated the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at first, while they were there, there were provocations. But later on when they left, when these special units left, it was worse.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long were you held on the pista?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was on the pista for more than a month, until they transferred me to the hangar. I was in the hangar then, but prior to that I spent all my time at the pista. In the hangar, I had lost all my strength from bad food, the fact that I didn't go to eat, that the food was bad, and I had no strength left. I feared going for lunch because we would be beaten, so I preferred to be hungry than to be beaten again.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So did something happen to you in the hangar that resulted in your being taken to Mujo's room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. What happened was that I didn't take food any more, so I lost consciousness. Then a friend learnt that I was not eating and they transferred me to Mujo's room. And there was this Predo who beat me most, who knocked out my teeth, and after that I didn't dare go to eat anymore. So I was half dead, and he carried me to Mujo's room. They gave me a drip, and it was thanks to my neighbour that I survived.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, when you went to Mujo's room and you were half dead, who gave you a drip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect, it was a doctor. Whether it was Esad Sadikovic or someone else, I didn't know them in person. But I think it was Esad Sadikovic. He gave me half a bottle of the drip and the other half to another elderly man. Where he got the infusion liquid from, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The doctor that treated you, was this person a detainee as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was also a detainee.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You've spoken of a drip or an infusion. Are you talking about some sort of liquid that was put into your vein using a needle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He put a needle, and this neighbour held the bottle in his hand until the dripping ended.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection as to approximately how long you were held in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly 20 days and more I was in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And then after that you were in Mujo's room for the rest of the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the camp was disbanded, I was in Mujo's room.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were in Omarska camp, were you ever interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was interrogated. When I went for interrogation, my turn came. Before that they asked for volunteers because they didn't beat or mistreat people at first. But then the beating started en masse at the interrogations so we avoided going for interrogation. But eventually my turn came. A guard said that I had to go. I didn't see who he was. I went there and stood in the corridor. Again I had to lean against the wall and spread my legs. He hit me on the back several times. I saw Nedzad Muslimovic. He was a young man. He had been beaten up and all bloody. And he pointed at him and said, "You tell everything you know or you'll end up like this." I stood there for a while and then I entered the office. Two unknown persons to me questioned us. And then this man wanted to hit me and he said "No, that's enough." Maybe he knew me by my father, who was well known. And I was already weak and he wouldn't let me -- let them beat me. He asked me whether I had responded to the mobilisation call. I said I had, that I went to Banja Luka, and I had my military booklet where they said that I had been discharged because of an ulcer. And then they continued questioning me normally and they wouldn't let the guard beat me. And when this guard took me back, he said, "You'll pay me for this," and I went back to the pista. As Drazenko Predojevic beat me most, I had boots on that he thought looked like military boots, and he hit me most. I'm always convinced that he was the guard who took me for interrogation. When I was at the pista I tried to be next to the wall. One day I didn't succeed, I was closer to the guard. He approached me suddenly, I didn't even see him. He hit me with his rifle butt and he knocked out my teeth, and from then I always avoided seeing this Drazenko because he was the one I feared most because I hadn't done anything. I wasn't guilty or anything, but he had something against me. And after that I was in the hangar, I didn't eat any food --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Let's stop for a moment, please, and go back to several things. You indicated that you were interrogated and that he took you and he beat you. When you say "he," do you know who it was who did this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think -- I learnt that that person's name was Drazenko Predojevic. No one else beat me except him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If I can interrupt you again. Did this beating occur before you were taken into the room for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This beating was before. And of course when you went to the restaurant, it was normal to be beaten --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Let's concentrate on the interrogation, okay? Now, you indicated that while you were in the interrogation room, someone tried to beat you and someone else said no. Who was it who stopped the person from beating you? Was it the interrogator or was it a guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The interrogator, he said that I shouldn't be beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: He said that you should not be beaten.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That everything was all right and that I shouldn't be beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Then when you were taken from the interrogation room, you said that someone said something to the effect that, "You will pay for this." Now, was that an interrogator, was that a guard, or do you not know who it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As he escorted me, I think it was that guard. I didn't dare look at him. But I'm convinced it was that same guard. And as Drazenko Predojevic beat me most, he had something against me, so I think it must have been him. And he also said I would pay for this. I don't know why I would pay. I never understood what he meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you said that a person, Drazenko Predojevic, beat you most. Did you know this person before you went to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I said I didn't know anyone in person. I learnt from the guards or from one of the detainees the names of these people. Whether they were the proper names, the real names, I don't know. We learned many nicknames.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether it was a guard or detainees who told you the name of Drazenko Predojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure of that, who told me. But in any event, I learnt that it was Drazenko Predojevic. Whether it was from the guards or someone else, I don't know. It was a long time ago. I learnt from others, either from the guards or from one of the prisoners, these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know how Drazenko would be dressed, what kind of clothing he wore in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He wore a police uniform, and once or twice he wore a military shirt. But mostly he wore a police uniform. Of course, it wasn't a camouflage police uniform but a regular police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you say that once or twice he wore a military shirt, what kind of military shirt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The usually SMB, olive-grey uniform or shirt.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So this shirt was not a camouflage shirt.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, while you were in the camp, what, if anything, did you learn about what shift Drazenko Predojevic worked on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learnt that, but much later. And I'm not sure now and I cannot say that he was in Krkan's or Krle's or Ckalja's shift, because all these things have gotten mixed up in my memory now, so I can't tell. I tried to think about those things less, because they torment me emotionally.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a Krkan, Krle, and Ckalja. Did you know any of these individuals before you went to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Let's start with Krkan. Did you ever know Krkan by any other name other than Krkan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know him personally; only by the name of Krkan. Later on I learnt his name -- his real name, but at the time I only knew him as Krkan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And how did you come to learn his name, Krkan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, from the guards, when they talked to one another, or from the detainees. That is how I learned his name, Krkan. He didn't introduce himself personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: As for Krle, did you know him by any other name other than Krle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Just Krle, by his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How did you learn his nickname, Krle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also in the same way as Krkan's: from the guards, from one of us detainees. That's how I learnt it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: As for Ckalja, did you know him by any other name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How did you learn his name, Ckalja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the same way as the previous two names, from the detainees or the guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned Krkan's shift, Krle's shift, Ckalja's shift. How did you come to learn that these shifts were known by those names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Amongst us detainees. And I noticed that they didn't have fixed positions. They would tour, the guards, and talk to them. They didn't have their own defined guard position. And so I learned that they were shift leaders.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So your observations were that guards had fixed positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. For instance, they would stand next to the "white house," to the entrance of the restaurant, around us. They had certain positions. He may walk up and down a little, whereas these three, they were always on the move, and I concluded from that that they were shift leaders. And when the guards came, the guards in a line, they would accompany them on the side, and that is on the basis of which I made my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You say when the guards came, they would accompany them on the side. Who would accompany them on the side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The shift leaders: Krle, Krkan, and Ckalja.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And when you say, "when the guards came," what are you talking about? Are you talking about shift changes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about shift changes. There were three shifts, and each lasted 12 hours, from 7.00 a.m. to 7.00 p.m., and from 7.00 p.m. to 7.00 a.m., and they would be working like that, and then they would be free for 24 hours. That's how the shifts changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, this kind of formation that you describe, where the guards are in a line and the shift commander is walking to the side of them, was that a formation that was familiar to you from your military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was similar to the way I used to do my guard duty. And I didn't see both shift leaders at the same time. Whether they had an assignment of posts in advance or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you say that this formation was similar to when you would do your guard duty. Was this when you were in charge of these six subordinates? Is that the time period you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about the time I did my military service in the Yugoslav People's Army. When we had to keep watch duty, that is how we had to act, in accordance with the rules of the Yugoslav People's Army, and I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So the leader, or the supervisor, would be on the side and the others would be in a line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a line, one by one or two by two. And of course, when you ended your guard duty, you would go back to the last position. But I didn't notice that in the camp. I didn't notice that at the camp, that system of rotation, that when you finished, you went to the end of the line.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated that you came to recognise these three individuals and know their names. While you were in Omarska camp, how often would you see Krkan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would see Krkan when his shift was on duty. If they worked during the daytime, I would see him from 7.00 a.m. to 7.00 p.m. I would see him passing by, around us, at the pista. When I was in Mujo's room, I saw him only once in the evening. He was at the entrance. At that moment a guard made a call-up of names of detainees to come out, and that is when I saw him at the entrance to Mujo's room. That guard called out --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If I could interrupt you. Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That guard called out some names, and they were told to pick up their things and to come out. And normally the announcement would be made that they would be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And is that the announcement that was made on that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was night-time. The night shift was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of those people who were called out on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember Asmir, who wasn't there at that time, Zlatan, and Esad. I knew those persons. And I was with Asmir in the hangar, and then I was moved to Mujo's room. After that I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, after these people were called out that night, did you ever see any of them again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw any of them again, of the three men.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you yourself have any knowledge as to whether they are still missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have knowledge from Asmir Cehic's wife. I never told her that he was called out because I didn't have the courage to do so. And he has an invalid child of 16 or 17, and that child used to walk, but now it is now an invalid. And so I did not have the courage to say that he was called out. I did not see him being taken away, but I know that his name was called out. And I've never had the courage to say that. I always said he stayed on after me; I didn't see him anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And the information from his wife, has he been reunited with his wife, or is he still missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, he is still missing; he still hasn't met up with his wife, been reunited with her. And two months ago, approximately, I talked to her, and she still had no knowledge of his whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, other than this one occasion when people were called out and Krkan was there, were there any other occasions you saw Krkan present when people were called out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that, apart from the time that I was in Mujo's room. But I didn't see him personally. There were roll-calls, depending on where you were. You tried to avoid being in their sight and being called out, so -- but I didn't -- as I say, I didn't see him personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you personally ever see Krkan engage in any mistreatment of detainees at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see him personally hit anyone. I did not see that, except for that roll-call when he was there on that occasion. But I didn't see him personally. As for his shift, there were terrible things. I didn't see him prevent guards from beating us or him beating anybody personally. I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned Krle. While you were on the pista, how often would you see Krle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If he worked during the day, the day shift, then I would see him on the pista, walking around and talking to the guards. In my opinion, that shift was one of the better ones. But there was an incident that took place, and I recall that. That is most vivid in my mind. I couldn't believe it --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you there. We'll talk about that, but not right at this moment. Now, after you moved from the pista, how often would you see Krle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Afterwards, when I was in that closed premises, I didn't see him often; when I was inside, not when I was outside. But while I was at the pista, I would see him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, very early in your testimony you indicated that the first night you were in the camp, Kvocka introduced himself and spoke to the detainees. Now, after that period, while you were on the pista, how often would you see Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would see Kvocka for about a month. During the day I would see him. He would walk around, talk to the guards, so I did see him. But I didn't notice anything on him. I didn't notice him doing anything else. I would just see him during the day five or six times. He would come down from the office, that kind of thing. So I'd see him talking to the guards, coming and going. I didn't follow him around, of course, but I did see him about. And this went on for about a month.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And after that month, you no longer saw him in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And you indicated that you would see him going about and talking to the guards. Did you ever see him enter any of the buildings in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I'm not sure I saw him. He went towards the "white house," for example, but I didn't actually see him go into the "white house." He would move around by the pista and hangar area. But as I say, I didn't follow him around, so I wasn't able to see him going in anywhere or beat somebody. I didn't see that, and I cannot state that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: During this time period when Kvocka was still in the camp, did you ever, on any occasions, observe dead bodies out in the open in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did see dead bodies close to the "white house." The "white house," as I'm sitting now, is to my right. I saw them there. And in the morning, after we had slept, up to the "red house", I saw some dead bodies there. And on one occasion, I saw one of my neighbours being carried out after being interrogated, and I recognised his jacket. He was a strongly-built man and I recognised him to be that person. And I did, of course, see bodies next to the "white house" or when we went to the toilet upstairs. And when we washed, on one occasion I saw dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, this person that you saw and recognised, who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted). We worked together in Celpak, my own company. And his turn for interrogation came and he went upstairs, and they carried him out of there and I think he was dead. And from that moment on, I never saw that person again.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, at this time I'd like to provide you with a photograph that's been taken of the model before you, and I'd like to ask you to identify some buildings and some locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: This would be the next exhibit in order, which should be 3/81.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Krstan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Madam Hollis has introduced a photograph which was Exhibit 3, but she didn't say whether it would be accepted into evidence and for identification purposes. We have a general objection to make that very frequently they are trying to put answers into the witness' mouth. That is a general observation and a general objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: As far as the exhibits are concerned, Your Honour, I thought that the procedure was that at the conclusion of the testimony, we would deal with all the exhibits. Secondly, as to the putting words into the mouth of the witness, the witness carried on with a very long discussion of events, and when I went back, I believe if you look at the transcript, you will see I didn't say anything other than what the witness had indicated, and it was for clarification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, your response.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Hollis gave numbers, assigned numbers to the previous two exhibits. The only exhibit which did not receive a number is this document. The next document was assigned a number. So technically this document was sidestepped in the records. So regardless of whether it will be tendered or not, I am afraid of some technical problems arising and that it has not been tendered as an exhibit and assigned a number, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I misspoke, this should be 3/82, and I perhaps misspoke and said "81." It should be 3/82, marked for identification at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: If not, we will repeat the same number to different documents. [Interpretation] I think it's clear. With respect to the file, we have already said that it would be a better idea to take all the documents together at the end of the examination-in-chief, or cross-examination, to avoid interruption, and this is true for the cross-examination by the Defence as well. At the end of everything, we're going to take all the documents together to facilitate matters and to speed up matters, so I think Madam Hollis was quite right there. As far as the other objection made by Mr. Krstan Simic is concerned, you can read the LiveNote, and if there are any specific objections on your part, we can deal with that. I don't think your objections are founded, but of course you do have the transcript, the LiveNote, and you can always correct it if you feel the need to do so. I would like to tell you that I prefer this mode of questioning; that is to say, to leave the witness to speak as freely as possible and then to go back to certain matters. It is true that she has to repeat what the witness has said in order to ask her question, but I think that that is preferable rather than ask short questions with short answers. I think that in the end, it is more spontaneous. The testimony is more spontaneous because the witness is allowed to speak freely, and afterwards, of course, we can go back to our specific questions. But, in any case, everybody has the right to choose his own method of examination. Of course, we can't induce answers, put words into the witness' mouth and infringe rights in this way. But having said that, thank you, Mr. Simic, for bringing that to our attention, and Madam Hollis, you have the floor to continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If that photograph could be shown to the witness and then put on the ELMO, please. Your Honours, I believe these are photos that I had previously provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, if you would just take a moment to look at that and familiarise yourself with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And then if it could be placed on the ELMO, please. Could you bring that forward so the other building shows. There's another building by the hangar. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you have spoken about the restaurant building, the administration building. Would you point to the building that you're referring to as the restaurant building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The restaurant building is this one here [indicates]. This is what we called the hangar [indicates]. This one here [indicates] is what we called the "white house," and that is the little red hut or house, and I referred to that as the "red house."

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You also talked about being held in an area you called the pista. Could you indicate to the Court this area that you call the pista?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is what we call the pista [indicates]. It is this area, this concrete slab area between the hangar and the restaurant. This is the area I was in [indicates], and I was always up against the wall here, the wall of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you saw bodies in several locations during the time period that Kvocka was still in the camp. Could you point to those areas and show the Judges where you saw those bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would see the bodies on this side of the "white house" [indicates], and once during the day, that is, one day that I was in the "white house," I spent one day in the "white house," and from one of the rooms I saw them behind -- dead bodies behind the "white house." And then when we went to sleep at night, if I wasn't in the restaurant, I was in the hangar, on the upper floor. And when we would go to the toilet in the morning, we would do that here [indicates], and I saw dead bodies next to this "red house" here.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could you again point to that area next to the "red house" and show where it was you saw these bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front of this here [indicates]. That's where I saw them, because the grass had been left to grow high there. But I saw the dead bodies there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And we went to the toilet there. We urinated there, and that's where I saw the dead bodies. I didn't recognise anybody, but I did see the dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The "red house" is the red house that is parallel to the "white house"; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but lower down.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you initially pointed at the "white house," you pointed to the side of the "white house" that is the side toward the restaurant building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I call the "red house".

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What about the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The "white house" is this one here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You pointed to bodies on the side of the "white house," that is, closer to the restaurant building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, closer to the restaurant. This is where the bodies were [indicates], and I could see them from the pista. And when I was inside the "white house," I could see it through the window. I saw bodies behind the "white house," dead bodies. And as I say, I was in the "white house" for one day.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you saw these dead bodies, how many dead bodies at a time would you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact number, but there were more than five or six bodies. I would see them here [indicates], bodies here [indicates], and bodies down there [indicates]. I don't know the exact number. I can't say I counted them, but more than five or six bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you saw these bodies, were you close enough that you could tell -- you could see any injuries to these bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw that they had been beaten up. I saw -- I remember one body. It was all black and blue and bloody. Whether that was from the beatings or whether he was killed -- whether he died from the beatings or whether he was killed by gunshot, I can't say, but that's what the body looked like. And they did not die a natural death, as they say.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, these bodies that you saw, how long were these bodies in these positions before they were removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would see a truck come by, and they would load the bodies onto the truck and take them away somewhere. I don't know where. This was one day, and the next day the bodies would be taken away.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, at this time I'd like you to look at a photograph, and this is an exhibit that has been previously marked. It is 3/37.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I do have copies for the Defence, and copies have, I believe, been provided for the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You said that bodies were taken away. By what type of vehicle were they taken away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a truck belonging to the mine. I call it Betonac, and it was orange in colour. And the bodies were placed to the back of the truck and taken off in an unknown direction. That's the truck [indicates] but before it had some wheels.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, if that could be put on the overhead, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So that's the type of truck you would see that would take away these bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the kind of truck I saw take away the bodies into some unknown direction; at least I didn't know where.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: There appears to be some writing on that truck. Could you tell us what that writing says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says "The mine of iron ore, Ljubija." It's not very clear on the picture, but that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned that you were held in the hangar building for a period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would ask if Exhibit 3/77 and, I believe it would be, 3/77C be provided to the witness. That is the ground floor of the hangar building. I have a copy of what I believe is 3/77C. If that would expedite matters, you could show this copy to the Defence. It is one part of the exhibit. It is the ground floor of the hangar building. If you could show that to the Defence first, please. With the Court's permission, I will use that copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like you for a moment to look at this diagram, and do you recognise that diagram?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it as the hangar, what I refer to as the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that after you were on the pista, you were held in the hangar for a period of time. What floor of the hangar were you held in? Was it the ground floor or the first floor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was on the ground floor, and I went through the large door, the garage door, and I was to the right of the wall, in that part of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, if that exhibit could be put on the ELMO, please, so that the witness can point to what he just described.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you went through a certain door and stayed in a certain place. Can you show us what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was here [indicates] at this first door, and I was in this section here [indicates] in the hangar. There was a sort of wire here, and there were people there before. But I was here [indicates]. And when I was in the hangar, I was so exhausted, I was here all the time in the hangar. And it was like some oil on the concrete floor, and that's where they were and I was. And when we had to go to the toilet, they would take us over there, but we always avoided going to the toilet because there were always beatings.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, you have pointed to an area that appears to be in this area that is marked "A1", and you point to an area that looks to be close to a wall. The wall that you're pointing toward, is that the wall that would have been facing toward the pista and the restaurant building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the wall, next to the pista and towards the restaurant building. I went in through this first door.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: This first door, you indicated, I believe, it was a large door. It's a large door into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a big door.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, while you were in the hangar, how many other people were in there with you in this area that you've indicated in A1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All this was full up [indicates], and this was a sort of wire fence and there were people here. I can't tell you the exact number, but there were a lot of us. I can't tell you the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you pointed toward what you call a wire or a fence area that appears to be close to the markings of A3, A4, A5, A6, A7. Is that where the fenced area is that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, here [indicates], this was the fenced-in area. Why it was fenced in, I don't know. But there was a wire sort of fence there, and those people were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: There were people inside the wire fence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The people were here as well

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: too.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated what your physical condition was while you were in the hangar. As far as the other individuals in this hangar area, what did you observe about their physical condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were in a similar state, depending on who they were. Some of them had bruises, black and blue. But they were all exhausted from hunger, from fear. We were all pale, long hair, we had beards. We looked awful. Even if you looked at yourself, when you would see yourself, you would get a fright. We were just skin and bone. Everybody had lost an enormous amount of weight from lack of food, from the beatings, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You also indicated that there was an area you would be taken to to go to the toilet. Can you show us again what area that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a door here [indicates] and there were some steps, and that was the toilet there [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What number is that? Is that number --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember. But that's where the toilet was. We would have to pass through this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Looking at the diagram, can you tell us what number is in that room that you've pointed to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's A11 or 6. I don't really know. The door was there, but I was very ill there and tried to move around as little as possible. But I do know that there were some steps there, and then you had to go up these steps to the WC. But as I say, I tried to move around as little as possible because I had no strength left, I was ill, so I didn't really remember the details. But I do know that I was there and I went to the toilet this away [indicates], but exactly what I did, how I went up this section, I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that people would try to avoid going to the toilet because they would be beaten. Who beat them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards beat them when they went to the toilet. Five or ten people would line up, and the guards would beat them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: On what shifts would these beatings occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Usually in Krkan's shift was when these beatings took place. It was this shift that beat most. The others did too, but these were particularly ferocious in their beatings, and we referred to it as Krkan's shift. They were terrible, those beatings, so we all tried to avoid going out and being seen as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, if people didn't go to the toilets to go to the bathroom, where did they relieve themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were receptacles of some kind, but they were all full. So if we had to pee, then we just pee'd where we were on the spot rather than go out, or they would just wet their pants rather than going out and being beaten. And I did this myself, I pee'd in my pants several times. I apologise for having to say that, but that's how it was. Or we would get dysentery, for example, and if you had dysentery, you didn't have much time to get to the toilet, so you would do what you had to do there too, on the way. That's what happened. They were terrible things. And as I say, I was too scared to go out, I was scared.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How would you describe the general conditions in the hangar, in the area that you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were terrible conditions. There was oil on the concrete floor. It was cold, and quite certainly we all had consequences from that damp concrete and everything else, because the conditions were atrocious in that part.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How did you get water while you were in the hangar building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you either had to go to the toilet or they brought us a canister. But we had to sing the songs, and they loved hearing us sing their songs.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What kind of songs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I remember still, and I tend to sing the song, "Who Says, Who Lies". That was one of the songs we would have to sing to get a bit of water. I got so used to singing it that sometimes even now I tend to slip into the song, the words of the song. It just happens of its own accord because it stuck in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what is that song, "Who Says, Who Lies"? What is the rest of it, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I feel a bit embarrassed to sing it for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You don't have to sing it. You can just tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Who is saying, who is lying, that Serbia is small. It is not small. It went to war three times." This song gave them strength and raised their morale.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So if you sang that song, were you then given sufficient amounts of water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we would get water. It depended on how many of us there were. There were cases where they would throw it through the window, and more of it would get spilled than we would be able to drink. There were cases when this happened. You had to sing louder and louder to get some water. A couple of times, I was at the pista and people who were in the garage were crying out for water, and they also had to sing. And the guards laughed and then they brought them water. These were terrible things.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When these people were crying out for water, how loudly were they crying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we were at the pista, they cried out so loudly that we could hear them, and this was in a closed room. And we might have been at the pista, so we heard them, so it meant that their cries were loud and their singing was loud. And to get water, they had to sing.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could ask one more question, I'll be finished with this area, and then after the break we can move to another area.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated that people were afraid to go to the bathroom because they would be beaten, so that they would urinate sometimes in their clothing, that they would have dysentery and defecate in their clothing. During the time you were at Omarska camp, how many times were you given the opportunity to wash yourself or your clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only once. They took us out to the grass between the "white house" and the small red hut. They took our clothes off, and they took powerful hoses and bathed us like that. And we were so weak that some men fell down. And when they fell down, they laughed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When they fell down, who laughed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the only time I had a bath. The guards bathed us and then they laughed. But we were so weak, and that is why people were falling down. People were beaten up, and they took it out on us.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You said that this time they hosed you down occurred between the "white house" and the small red building. Is that the same red building you pointed to earlier where you saw bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe we can pause for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Madam Hollis. We are going to have a half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Ms. Hollis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, in your testimony you've already given, you indicated that in the beginning people would volunteer to be interrogated and then after some time they stopped volunteering to be interrogated. Now, initially why would people volunteer to be interrogated, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no beatings and some people were in fact returned home, and that's why we hoped they would establish that we had no guilt and they would send us home. However, later when the beating started, we all avoided going for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long had you been in the camp when the beatings started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say something like 10 or 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, when did the interrogations begin in the camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately after we arrived at the camp, I think it was a Monday, they came in a small minibus in the morning, and then they stayed all day.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the time you were at the camp, what differences in treatment of the detainees, if any, did you notice between the time the interrogators were in the camp and the periods of time that they were not in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a difference. At least I at the pista didn't notice anyone being beaten, but later on when they went upstairs they were beaten. We on the pista were not beaten so badly. While the investigators were there, there was not so much mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So what period of the day did most of the mistreatment occur, based on your observations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went for interrogation. And then if something happened, if somebody got killed at the front and they were angry, then they would beat, and also when we went for food they beat us en masse. These beatings occurred then. When we went for food, then they would beat us.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask the witness to speak closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could you please try to move up closer to the microphone, and if you could try to speak slowly and very clearly. Thank you. When did you first get food after you arrived at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got food for the first time on the third or fourth day. Once when my turn came, the food ran out. So it wasn't until my third or fourth day that I got some food for the first time, a piece of bread and some liquid soup with some cabbage inside and some beans. There were 30 in a group, and we had to go and get our meal and come back as quickly as possible. We had to run back. There were cases later, if the first man didn't take his proper seat at the table, we had to go back as quickly as possible. The time given was very short, so I can't tell you exactly when this was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, these beatings that people received when they went to get their meals, when did those beatings begin? How long had you been in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly but they started early on. Not at the very first, but later on. I can't tell you how many days went by. I can't remember when the beatings started.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, when you went for meals, was this during daylight hours or was it at night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the day. It depended when the pista group came. People came from the hangar, from Mujo's room. Sometimes it happened at 4.00 in the afternoon. So it depended. There wasn't a fixed time for meals; it depended on the order of the groups and when your turn came.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you have testified about being very badly beaten and being in very poor physical condition. When did your beatings begin? When did you first begin to get beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My beating started -- when you pass through the corridor, a guard might hit you, give you a blow or two, but that was not so important. The worst period for me was after the interrogation. Whether it was this Drazenko Predojevic who said, "You went to fight. You have those boots on your feet," and whether it was because of that, that was when I was beaten so badly. But before that it wasn't so important.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you said that your beatings started when you would pass through the corridor. You would pass through the corridor going where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we ran along the corridor to go into the restaurant, to get our meals.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long had you been in the camp when you first began to get those beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just said, 10 or 15 days later. I don't know exactly how much time I had spent in the camp when those beatings started.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you've testified about the beating you received when you were interrogated, and after that you testified that you were on the pista and "he" beat you and did things to you. This beating you're talking about on the pista after you were interrogated, who did that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I later learnt that his name was Drazenko Predojevic, and I always avoided him when he was on duty. He would hit me whenever he saw me, with a stick or whatever. And once when I came from the hangar, I didn't manage to get a place next to the wall because I always tried to be as close to the wall as possible so I wouldn't be so visible. On that day I was closer to him and he recognised me. He hit me unexpectedly with his rifle butt, or rifle, I don't know. He hit me a couple of times and then he left, and then I lost all my teeth. So I avoided him as much as I could whenever he was around; I laid down so he wouldn't see me. And whenever he was on duty, I never went for my meals.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you also testified that in the hangar you passed out and you were taken to Mujo's room and that you were in very bad physical condition. How long were you in Mujo's room before you were able to leave that room to go for food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was between five and ten days. I got this infusion, and then the guards would allow some food to be brought to those people who couldn't go for their meals. So I don't know exactly how long it was before I was able to go for meals.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You testified about getting this infusion from a detainee who was a doctor. Other than this care, did you receive any medical care for the injuries you received in Omarska while you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no medical care, except for that infusion, in that case. Especially later on, I avoided appearing and people seeing me. I didn't ask for any assistance, and I didn't get any medical care, except for that drip given by the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you testified about seeing other people who were abused. Did you ever observe any of them receiving medical care while they were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally did not see anyone receiving medical care. Possibly somebody did get it but I didn't see it. I didn't get any.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You testified that on one occasion you were in the "white house" and you saw dead bodies behind the "white house" from the room that you were in. The room that you were in in the "white house," what did you observe about that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That day, it was daytime, it suddenly started raining, I think, and I had to enter the "white house." I was afraid. The first room was for the wounded or something, and there was only one man there. Then straight ahead was the toilet. I went to the right, the last room on the right, and when I entered it was covered in blood, the walls and the window.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You have testified that you never saw Kvocka engage in any physical abuse of prisoners. During the time that you were detained in Omarska, do you recall ever seeing him present when detainees were called out and abused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember one time I was at the pista --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Before you explain what you saw, sir, let me ask you just a couple of preliminary questions, if I may. Now, you've indicated you were at the pista when this incident occurred. What time of the day or night was it, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was 5.00 or 6.00 at night. It was still daylight because it was summer. So it was in the afternoon. I didn't have a watch, but as far as I can recollect, it was around that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: At this time, do you have any recollection of how long you had been in the camp when this incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe some 20 days, more or less. I'm not 100 per cent sure, but about that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, if you would tell the Court about this incident, and start with what you first saw or heard that captured your attention and then if you would very slowly and clearly tell the Court what you observed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were sitting on the pista. No one was being mistreated. And I saw Kvocka talking in front of the restaurant. Then I heard a voice, people being called out. I saw a man whom I don't know. He was calling out names, "Asaf, Kiki, Rezak, Began." I didn't even see that man well, nor do I know him or remember him. And when I saw him coming up, Kvocka turned around and went in the opposite direction in relation to the man who was approaching. After a short time, we were ordered to lie down on the pista, to lie on our stomachs. And I noticed, I don't know how, I saw Kiki going to the "white house." I didn't see anyone else then. I heard the noise made by guards going there, but I only saw Kiki.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, before you go on from there, if I could ask you some questions. This man who was calling out these names, you said, "Kiki, Rezak, and Began," how loudly was this man calling out these names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very loudly, too loudly, so we heard those names very well. He was yelling those names out. And I seem to remember hearing "Kikica, Zigica needs you." We knew that something was about to happen whenever there was a call-out of names. I was looking towards the restaurant, and at that moment Kvocka was leaving. I didn't see anything else because we were ordered to lie down face down, and I didn't see anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, Kiki, did you know a man named Kiki before you came to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did know him because he had a barbershop, and that is how I knew him. I would go and visit him for his services but I didn't know him as a friend. I would just go and have a haircut or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did he have this barbershop? In what town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Prijedor, in the centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know him by any other name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were told to lie down on your stomachs and you saw Kiki going toward the "white house." Is this the Kiki that you're referring to, the man who had the barbershop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the Kiki I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know a man called Began before coming to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did because he had a coffee bar. I would drop by after work, have a beer or something. We also were not friends. I don't know whether he knew me in person, but I knew him because he owned this cafe and I would visit it, and that is how I knew him from before.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know Began by any name other than "Began"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I just know him under the name Began.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know a man by the name of (redacted) before you came to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew him a little better because he was involved with music, and we used to play table tennis often. He would come to our club. I would pass by his house when I went to work, and I knew his name and surname, (redacted). I would pass by his house on the way to work, and he would come to the local community offices where we played table tennis often.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You said that you were on your stomach, you saw Kiki going towards the "white house" and that you heard noise from guards. What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard noise, screams, moans. That's what I heard. These were terrible screams. How many men there were inside, I don't know. Who was there, I really don't know. But I just heard those screams. After a short while I saw Kiki going back. Again I saw only him. He was all bloodied. Where he went, as far as I could see, he went towards the restaurant. But we were lying face down and no one dared move. If anybody moved, he would get hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, this noise, these screams, and these moans that you heard, where did this noise, screams, and moans seem to be coming from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
